title: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa
content: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say. Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast. The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum. This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details. The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged". It said that the new policy would still abide by the Constitutional Court ruling. South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries. Thursday's demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said. In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications. Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors. "There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported," he added. Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers. Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property. In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals. Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported. Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence. The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction. The latest unrest follows a July ruling by Constitutional Court, South Africa's highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines. The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents. This prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration. Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status. Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa. Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks. Earlier this year, anti-immigration groups staged weeks of demonstrations demanding that undocumented foreign nationals leave the country by 30 June . The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities. title: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee
content: As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold. "It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat. With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far. "There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this." Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand. "Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said. "Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads." After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation". The attacks, he said, were "tearing Kyiv apart" . Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too. "I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says. Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision. A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided. "People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter." Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding. For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent. Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope. "Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK." The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties. "We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says. The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation. Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking. "Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling." Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland. "Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says. For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside. Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital. "I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains. "Everything that can be a Russian target." On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door. In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home. The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation. At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most. "After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good." Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her. "She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains. Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad. Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before. The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts. Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid. The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks. But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing. Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school. "They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says. Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk and Anastasiia Levchenko. The charity came to national attention in October 2023 when Catherine visited the hub. It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul. Five children are among the victims of a strike that destroyed 30 flats in northern Ukraine as families slept. The club's chair praises people's "phenomenal" generosity, which he says "makes it all worthwhile". It is not clear who is behind the attacks which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea as part of its war against Ukraine. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC
content: A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was authorised by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency. In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time. Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle". Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent". A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head. But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her. He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut. Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych. For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent. Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev. He understood it was an official mission. "As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says. Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead. Reut then communicated directly with Berezovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives. The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies. The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer". Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep. It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force. Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack. He called for "the truth, protection, and justice". Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol. She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine. Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting. The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling. The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories. They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine. Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine. Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case. Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us. He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea. "In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison. Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia. But might this story be even murkier? At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present. At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised". "Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining. The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court. Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets. When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason. As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own. The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son. Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia. He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation". Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair. Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained. Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko.
